prompt: The risk-free rate is 2.5% and the expected market risk premium is 5.5%. The stock of Nordlicht AG has a beta of 1.3. Under the CAPM, what is its required return? Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
E(R) = rf + β × (E(R_M) − rf) = 2.5% + 1.3 × 5.5% = 9.65%.
The premium (5.5%), not E(R_M), multiplies beta.

steps.title: The CAPM formula
steps.why: Required return = risk-free rate + beta × market risk premium. The market risk premium is E(R_M) − rf.

pitfalls: Multiplying beta with E(R_M) instead of the premium – here the premium (5.5%) is already given.

prompt: A stock has a volatility of 35% and a correlation of 0.45 with the market. The market has a volatility of 18% and an expected return of 8.5%; the risk-free rate is 2.5%. Compute the stock's beta and its expected return under the CAPM. Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
β = ρ × σ_i/σ_M = 0.45 × 35%/18% = 0.8750.
E(R) = 2.5% + 0.8750 × (8.5% − 2.5%) = 7.75%.
Although the stock is almost twice as volatile as the market, its beta is below 1.

steps.title: Beta from correlation and volatilities
steps.why: Beta measures only the part of the stock's risk that moves with the market: correlation × (stock volatility / market volatility).

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.why: The stock is almost twice as volatile as the market, but its beta is below 1: most of its risk is idiosyncratic and is not rewarded.

pitfalls: Using σ_i / σ_M as beta without multiplying by the correlation.

prompt: You invest 60% of your money in Fast Semiconductor (beta 2.25) and 40% in the risk-free asset. The risk-free rate is 4% and the market risk premium 6%. What are the beta and the expected return of your portfolio? Report percentages with two decimals.

steps.title: Portfolio beta
steps.why: The beta of a portfolio is the weighted average of the betas. The risk-free asset has beta 0.

steps.title: Expected return
lines: E(Rp) = rf + βp × market risk premium

pitfalls: Giving the risk-free asset a beta of 1 instead of 0.

prompt: The expected return of Chambersburg Forging is 12%. The risk-free rate is 4% and the expected market return 12.5%. What is the beta of the stock according to the CAPM?
pitfalls: Dividing by E(R_M) = 12.5% instead of the market risk premium 8.5%.

prompt: You hold only an ETF on the market portfolio (expected return 11%, volatility 18%); the risk-free rate is 2.5%. Your broker suggests adding Lumen Corp: expected return 4%, volatility 15%, correlation zero with the market. (a) What is Lumen's beta and its required return? (b) What is its alpha – should you add it? Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
(a) β = ρ σ_i/σ_M = 0 → required return = rf + 0 × 8.5% = 2.5%.
(b) α = 4% − 2.5% = 1.5% > 0 → the stock lies above the SML; adding a little of it raises your Sharpe ratio. Its low stand-alone return does not matter, only its return relative to the risk it adds (none, since ρ = 0). It lies below the CML (a single stock with only idiosyncratic risk) but above the SML: it is undervalued.

steps.title: (a) Beta
steps.why: Correlation with the market is zero → beta is zero, however volatile the stock is.

steps.title: (b) Alpha
steps.why: Alpha = expected return − required return. A positive alpha means the stock lies above the security market line.

steps.title: (b) Should you add it?
steps.why: Yes. Adding a little of a positive-alpha stock raises the Sharpe ratio of your portfolio. Its low stand-alone return does not matter – what matters is the return relative to the market risk it adds (none). It lies below the CML (a single stock with only idiosyncratic risk), but above the SML: it is undervalued.

pitfalls: Rejecting the stock because 4% is below the market's 11%.

prompt: The market portfolio has an expected return of 10% and a volatility of 25%; the risk-free rate is 2.5%. (a) What is the slope of the capital market line (CML)? (b) What is the slope of the security market line (SML)? (c) What is the expected return of an efficient portfolio with a volatility of 15%?
modelAnswer:
(a) CML slope = Sharpe ratio of M = (10% − 2.5%)/25% = 0.30 (return per unit of volatility).
(b) SML slope = market risk premium = 10% − 2.5% = 7.5% (return per unit of beta).
(c) On the CML: 2.5% + 0.30 × 15% = 7.00%.

steps.title: (a) Slope of the CML
steps.why: The CML plots expected return against volatility. Its slope is the Sharpe ratio of the market: extra return per unit of volatility.

steps.title: (b) Slope of the SML
steps.why: The SML plots expected return against beta. Its slope is the market risk premium: extra return per unit of beta.

steps.title: (c) Efficient portfolio with 15% volatility
steps.why: Efficient portfolios lie on the CML.

pitfalls: Mixing up the axes: the CML uses volatility, the SML uses beta.

prompt: rf = 4%, E(R_M) = 10%, σ_M = 16%. Stock A has a volatility of 24% and a correlation of 0.4 with the market. (a) What is A's beta and expected return? (b) What does an efficient portfolio (on the CML) with the same volatility as A earn? Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
(a) β = 0.4 × 24%/16% = 0.60 → E = 4% + 0.6 × 6% = 7.60%.
(b) 4% + (6%/16%) × 24% = 13.00%.
The gap shows that most of A's volatility is idiosyncratic and therefore not rewarded.

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.why: Same volatility, but 13% vs 7.6%: most of A's volatility is idiosyncratic. Only the market part (beta) earns a premium.

pitfalls: Putting stock A on the CML – single stocks lie on the SML, only efficient portfolios lie on the CML.

prompt: A gold-mining stock has a beta of −0.25. The risk-free rate is 3% and the expected market return 9%. What is its required return, and why can it be below the risk-free rate? Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
E(R) = 3% + (−0.25) × 6% = 1.50%.
A negative-beta stock tends to rise when the market falls: it insures the portfolio, so investors accept an expected return below rf.

steps.title: Why below the risk-free rate?
steps.why: A negative beta means the stock tends to rise when the market falls. It acts like insurance for the portfolio, so investors accept an expected return even below the risk-free rate.

prompt: (a) What are the expected return and the volatility of the market portfolio (a 50–50 combination of the two portfolios)? Report percentages with two decimals.

steps.title: Expected return of the market
steps.why: The market is 50% green and 50% brown (equal total value).

steps.title: Variance of the market – term by term

pitfalls: Taking the average of the volatilities (21%) – that ignores the diversification from ρ = 0.5.

prompt: (b) Compute the beta of the green portfolio with respect to the market and its required return under the CAPM. Does the CAPM hold in this economy?
modelAnswer:
Cov(G, M) = Cov(G, 0.5G + 0.5B) = 0.5 × 0.18² + 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.18 × 0.24 = 0.0270.
β_G = 0.0270/0.033300 = 0.8108 → required return = 2% + 0.8108 × 10.50% = 10.51%.
The green portfolio offers only 10% → negative alpha (≈ -0.51%). Not every asset lies on the SML, so the market portfolio is not efficient and the CAPM does not hold (e.g. because investors care about sustainability, not only mean and variance).

steps.title: Covariance of green with the market
steps.why: The market is 0.5 G + 0.5 B, so Cov(G, M) = 0.5 × Var(G) + 0.5 × Cov(G, B).

steps.title: Does the CAPM hold?
steps.why: Green stocks only offer 10%, slightly less than the 10.51% the CAPM requires: alpha ≈ −0.51%. If an asset is off the SML, the market portfolio is not efficient, so the CAPM does not hold – e.g. because investors also care about sustainability, not only mean and variance.
steps.result: No – green has a negative alpha of about −0.51%

pitfalls: Using Var(G) instead of Var(M) as the denominator of beta.

prompt: Compare the capital market line (CML) and the security market line (SML): axes, slope, and which assets lie on each line.
modelAnswer: CML: expected return against volatility (total risk); slope = Sharpe ratio of the market (E(R_M) − rf)/σ_M; only efficient portfolios (mixes of the market and the risk-free asset) lie on it, single stocks lie below because their idiosyncratic risk is not rewarded. SML: expected return against beta (market risk); slope = market risk premium E(R_M) − rf; in equilibrium every stock and portfolio lies on it. Above the SML = positive alpha (buy), below = negative alpha (sell).
keyPoints: CML: x-axis volatility, slope Sharpe ratio of M
Only efficient portfolios on the CML; stocks below
SML: x-axis beta, slope market risk premium
Every asset on the SML in equilibrium (alpha = 0)
